All three are anilines, so the basicity is decided by what the **para substituent** does to
the nitrogen lone pair.
**(III) p-Toluidine**, with a **–CH₃** group. Methyl **releases** electrons (+I and
hyperconjugation), pushing density into the ring and so towards the nitrogen. The lone pair
is more available ⟹ **most basic**, pKb **8·92**
**(I) Aniline**, unsubstituted. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring, but nothing makes
it worse ⟹ intermediate, pKb **9·38**
**(II) p-Nitroaniline**, with a **–NO₂** group. Nitro withdraws electrons strongly, both
inductively and by **resonance**, and from the **para** position that resonance reaches the
amino nitrogen directly, draining the lone pair away ⟹ **least basic**, pKb **13·0**
So basicity runs **III > I > II**, and in **increasing** order:
**II < I < III** ✓ — option (c)
The size of the nitro effect is worth noting: p-nitroaniline is some four thousand times
weaker a base than aniline, because the –NO₂ group can accept the lone pair into its own
resonance structures. The methyl group, working only through induction, shifts things by a
mere factor of three.
The general rule: **electron-releasing groups strengthen an aromatic amine, electron-
withdrawing groups weaken it**, and the effect is largest when the group is ortho or para,
where resonance can operate.
∴ II < I < III.

Note: the printed key gives (b), III < II < I, which places p-toluidine as the weakest base
and aniline as the strongest. A methyl group strengthens a base and a nitro group weakens
it, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|28|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
A Brønsted base donates its lone pair to a proton, so the strongest is the one whose lone
pair is most **available** — not delocalised, and not shielded.
**(c) N-Methylpyrrole** ✗ is the **weakest** of all, not the strongest. Pyrrole is
**aromatic**, and its aromaticity depends on the nitrogen lone pair being part of the
six-electron π sextet. Donating that pair to a proton would **destroy the aromaticity**, so
it is essentially unavailable. Pyrroles are barely basic at all.
**(a) Triethylamine** and **(b) Dimethylamine** are ordinary aliphatic amines, with pKa of
the conjugate acid about 10·75 and 10·7 respectively. Triethylamine's three ethyl groups
release electrons, but they also crowd the nitrogen, so steric hindrance cancels much of the
gain.
**(d) Quinuclidine** ✓ **strongest.** It is a **bicyclic** tertiary amine with the nitrogen at
a bridgehead. The three alkyl groups all contribute their +I effect, exactly as in
triethylamine — but because they are **tied back into a rigid cage**, the lone pair points
outward and is completely **unhindered**. It gets the electronic benefit of a tertiary amine
without the steric penalty, and its conjugate acid has pKa **11·0**, the highest here.
The comparison of quinuclidine with triethylamine is the standard illustration that **steric
hindrance, not electronics, is what holds ordinary tertiary amines back**.
∴ option (d).

Note: the printed key gives (c). An N-methylpyrrole has its lone pair locked into the
aromatic sextet and is the least basic of the four, so the key is wrong and has been
corrected to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|29|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The rule to apply is
**the strongest conjugate acid comes from the weakest base**
so find the weakest of the four parent amines and its ammonium ion is the answer.
The parent amines are:
**(a) cyclohexylamine** — a plain aliphatic amine, **strongly** basic (pKb ≈ 3·3)
**(d) methylamine** — also strongly basic (pKb 3·4)
**(c) benzylamine** — the ring is insulated by a –CH₂–, so it too behaves as an aliphatic
amine (pKb 4·7)
**(b) aniline** — the nitrogen is attached **directly** to the ring, so its lone pair is
**delocalised into the π system**. Much the **weakest** base of the four (pKb 9·4)
Therefore the **anilinium ion**, C₆H₅NH₃⁺, is the **strongest conjugate acid** ✓ — option (b).
The numbers confirm it. The pKa values of the conjugate acids are
anilinium **4·6**, benzylammonium 9·3, methylammonium 10·6, cyclohexylammonium 10·7
and the lower the pKa the stronger the acid.
The reason anilinium gives up its proton so readily is the mirror image of why aniline is a
weak base: losing the proton **restores the delocalisation** of the nitrogen lone pair into
the ring, which is a stabilising reward that the aliphatic ions do not get.
Option (c) is the trap — benzylamine looks aromatic, but the CH₂ spacer blocks any
resonance.
∴ option (b).

Note: the printed key gives (d), the methylammonium ion. Methylamine is a strong base, so
its conjugate acid is weak; aniline is the weakest base here and anilinium the strongest
acid, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|33|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Pyrrole's nitrogen contributes its **lone pair to the aromatic sextet**, and the consequence
is that electron density is pushed **out onto the carbon atoms** of the ring.
Draw the resonance structures. The nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the ring, and the
negative charge appears in turn at **C-2, C-3, C-4 and C-5**, with the nitrogen carrying a
positive charge. Counting the structures shows the charge is concentrated at the two
positions adjacent to nitrogen — the **α-positions, C-2 and C-5** ✓ — option (d).
The electron density there is **greater than in benzene**, which is why pyrrole is described
as an **electron-rich** (π-excessive) heterocycle and why it undergoes electrophilic
substitution far more readily than benzene does — nitration, halogenation and sulphonation
all occur under much milder conditions.
And they occur **at C-2**. The reason is the stability of the intermediate: attack at the
α-position gives an arenium ion stabilised by **three** resonance structures, while attack at
C-3 gives only **two**. Pyrrole brominates to 2-bromopyrrole, and the Reimer–Tiemann
reaction gives pyrrole-2-carbaldehyde.
Because the lone pair is committed to the ring in this way, it is **not available for
protonation**, which is why pyrrole is an exceptionally **weak base** — the subject of the
companion question on the same page.
∴ 2 and 5.

The **carbylamine (isocyanide) test** is given by **primary amines only** — aliphatic or
aromatic — when warmed with chloroform and alcoholic KOH:
R–NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH ⟶ **R–NC** + 3KCl + 3H₂O
The isocyanide formed has an extremely offensive smell, and that smell is the positive test.
The reaction needs **two hydrogens on the nitrogen**, because the attacking species is
dichlorocarbene (:CCl₂) and both N–H hydrogens are lost as HCl in the course of the
mechanism. Secondary and tertiary amines have fewer than two and give no reaction.
So classify the options:
**(a) N,N-Dimethylaniline**, C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂ — nitrogen carries two methyls and a phenyl, **no
hydrogen**. **Tertiary** ✗
**(b) Triethylamine**, (C₂H₅)₃N — three ethyls, no hydrogen. **Tertiary** ✗
**(c) N-Methylaniline**, C₆H₅NH(CH₃) — one methyl, one phenyl, **one** hydrogen.
**Secondary** ✗
**(d) p-Methylbenzylamine**, CH₃–C₆H₄–CH₂–NH₂ — nitrogen carries one carbon group and **two**
hydrogens. **Primary** ✓ **gives the test** ✓
The test is in fact the standard way of **detecting** a primary amine in qualitative organic
analysis, precisely because it is so selective — and so unpleasant that it is unmistakable.
∴ p-methylbenzylamine.

Note: the printed key gives (a), N,N-dimethylaniline, which is a tertiary amine with no N–H
bond at all. Only the primary amine responds, so the key is wrong and has been corrected
to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|43|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Work backwards from the last clue, which is the most specific.
**Clue 3 — C on reduction gives isopropylmethylamine, (CH₃)₂CH–NH–CH₃.**
Reducing an **isocyanide** R–NC adds four hydrogens and gives a **secondary** amine
R–NH–CH₃, where the methyl comes from the isocyanide carbon. So
R–NH–CH₃ = (CH₃)₂CH–NH–CH₃ ⟹ **R = isopropyl**, and C is isopropyl isocyanide,
(CH₃)₂CH–NC.
**Clue 2 — A with CHCl₃ and caustic potash gives C.** That is the **carbylamine reaction**,
which works only on **primary** amines and converts R–NH₂ into R–NC. Since C is
(CH₃)₂CH–NC, **A must be (CH₃)₂CH–NH₂, isopropylamine** ✓
**Clue 1 — A with nitrous acid gives an alcohol and evolves N₂.** This confirms it: only a
**primary aliphatic** amine behaves that way, forming an unstable diazonium ion that at once
loses nitrogen to leave an alcohol.
**Check the formula:** (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ is **C₃H₉N** ✓ as given.
The other options fail the primary-amine test: **(b)** and **(c)** are secondary and tertiary
amines, which give no carbylamine reaction, and **(d)** n-propylamine, although primary and
also C₃H₉N, would give **n-propyl**methylamine on the same sequence, not the isopropyl
compound.
So the branching in the final product is what distinguishes (a) from (d).
∴ (CH₃)₂CH–NH₂.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|63|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two steps, and the second is the one that matters.
**Step 1 — diazotisation.** Aniline with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0 °C gives
**V = benzenediazonium chloride**, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻. The low temperature keeps it from
decomposing.
**Step 2 — azo coupling with β-naphthol in NaOH.** The diazonium ion is a **weak**
electrophile, so it can only attack a ring that is strongly activated. β-Naphthol qualifies,
and the alkali makes it better still by converting the –OH into the even more strongly
activating **–O⁻**.
**Where does it attack?** The hydroxyl is at **C-2**, and it directs to the positions ortho
and para to itself. In 2-naphthol the available **ortho** position is **C-1**, and that is
where coupling occurs — it is the most reactive site in the molecule.
The product is therefore **1-(phenylazo)-2-naphthol**: the azo bridge at C-1 with the
hydroxyl **next to it** at C-2 ✓ — which is the structure drawn in option (a).
The distractors each put the azo group in the wrong place relative to the OH — option (d)
separates them by a carbon, and (b) and (c) place them on the wrong positions altogether.
This is the chemistry of the **azo dyes**. The extended conjugation through the –N=N– bridge
is what makes them intensely coloured, and 1-(phenylazo)-2-naphthol is an orange-red solid.
Coupling with a **phenol** needs mildly alkaline conditions, as here; coupling with an
**amine** needs mildly acidic ones.
∴ option (a).

Note: the printed key gives (d), which places the azo group one carbon away from the
hydroxyl. Coupling occurs ortho to the activating group, at C-1 of 2-naphthol, so the key is
wrong and has been corrected to (a).

Converting an alcohol to an alkyl chloride with **dry HCl** needs a catalyst, and the one
used is **anhydrous zinc chloride** ✓ — option (c). The mixture of concentrated HCl with
anhydrous ZnCl₂ is the **Lucas reagent**.
Zinc chloride is a **Lewis acid**. It coordinates to the oxygen of the alcohol, which makes
the –OH a far better leaving group:
R–OH + ZnCl₂ ⟶ R–O(H)–ZnCl₂ ⟶ R⁺ + [Zn(OH)Cl₂]⁻
and the chloride then captures the carbocation. Without the catalyst, hydroxide is too poor
a leaving group and the reaction barely proceeds.
The same reagent is the basis of the **Lucas test** for distinguishing the three classes of
alcohol by how fast the insoluble chloride appears:
**tertiary** — turbidity **immediately**
**secondary** — in about five minutes
**primary** — no reaction at room temperature
Why not the others:
**(a) anhydrous AlCl₃** and **(b) anhydrous FeCl₃** are Lewis acids too, but they are the
catalysts for **Friedel–Crafts** reactions and ring halogenation of arenes, not for this.
**(d) Cu powder** is a catalyst in the direct synthesis of chlorosilanes and in some coupling
reactions, not here.
The word **anhydrous** matters: any water would hydrate the zinc chloride and destroy its
Lewis acidity.
∴ anhydrous ZnCl₂.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|6|Pradeep Chemistry:
All four reagents will convert an alcohol into an alkyl halide, so the question is which is
**best** — and 'best' here means the cleanest product and the easiest work-up.
**(c) SOCl₂ in the presence of pyridine** ✓ — the **Darzens procedure**:
R–OH + SOCl₂ --pyridine--> **R–Cl** + **SO₂↑** + **HCl↑**
Both by-products are **gases**. They escape from the reaction mixture, leaving the alkyl
chloride essentially pure, with no distillation or separation required. The pyridine is there
to mop up the HCl and keep the mixture from turning strongly acidic.
The others all leave something behind:
**(a) PCl₃** gives R–Cl together with **H₃PO₃**, phosphorous acid, a liquid that must be
separated from the product.
**(b) PCl₅** gives R–Cl with **POCl₃**, again a liquid by-product, and PCl₅ is also harsher —
it can cause side reactions.
**(d) Dry HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂** works, but it proceeds through a **carbocation**, so
primary alcohols react poorly and secondary and tertiary ones are liable to
**rearrangement**, giving a mixture.
The thionyl chloride route also goes with **retention** of configuration at a chiral carbon
when pyridine is absent, by the SNi mechanism — another reason it is the preferred
laboratory method.
∴ SOCl₂ in presence of pyridine.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry:
Bromination with **Br₂ in light (hv)** is a **free-radical substitution**, and the bromine
atom is highly **selective**: it attacks whichever C–H bond gives the **most stable radical**.
The order of radical stability is
**tertiary > secondary > primary**
so the tertiary C–H is attacked overwhelmingly. Bromine is far more selective than chlorine
in this respect — the tertiary position is favoured by a factor of about 1600 to 1 over a
primary one, which is why a single product dominates.
In **methylcyclopentane** the ring carbon bearing the methyl group is attached to **three**
other carbons — two ring carbons and the methyl — and its single hydrogen is therefore the
only **tertiary** C–H in the molecule. That is where the bromine goes:
**1-bromo-1-methylcyclopentane** ✓ — the structure in option (c), with the Br and the CH₃ on
the **same** ring carbon.
The other options put the bromine at less favourable sites:
**(a)** on the methyl group — a **primary** carbon
**(b)** on the ring carbon next to the methyl — **secondary**
**(d)** on a ring carbon further round — also **secondary**
All three would be formed in traces, but none is the major product.
The contrast worth remembering: **chlorination** is much less selective and would give a
mixture of all four, which is why bromination is used when one product is wanted.
∴ option (c).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|18|Pradeep Chemistry:
The dipole moment of a molecule is the **vector sum** of its bond moments, so both the bond
polarity and the **symmetry** matter.
The measured values are
**CH₃Cl 1·86 D** ✓ highest
CH₂Cl₂ 1·60 D
CHCl₃ 1·03 D
CCl₄ **0 D**
**CCl₄** is easiest: four identical C–Cl bonds pointing to the corners of a **regular
tetrahedron** cancel exactly, so the molecule is **non-polar** despite four very polar bonds.
For the other three, the question is why the dipole **falls** as chlorines are added, when
each new C–Cl bond is itself polar.
In **CH₃Cl** there is a single C–Cl moment pointing one way, reinforced slightly by the three
C–H moments pointing the other. Nothing opposes it.
Adding a second chlorine, as in CH₂Cl₂, introduces a C–Cl moment at the **tetrahedral angle**
to the first, so the two **partly cancel**; the resultant is smaller than one bond moment
would suggest.
In **CHCl₃** three C–Cl moments oppose one another further still, leaving a smaller resultant
along the single C–H axis.
So the more symmetrical the molecule becomes, the more the bond moments cancel — and
chloromethane, the least symmetrical, has the largest dipole.
∴ CH₃Cl.
